title: Data Engineering Fundamentals
tagline: Model, transform, test and run data pipelines, with live SQL on raw, messy data
summary: Learn what holds across every data platform: how data is modelled for analytics (star schemas and slowly changing dimensions), how raw data is cleaned in layers with SQL (deduplication, latest records, incremental loads, quality tests), and how pipelines are designed, scheduled, monitored, secured and costed. You practise the SQL for all of it, live in your browser, on a raw order-event log with duplicates, late events, customers who move city and a messy payments feed. Python, Spark, Airflow and Kafka are explained with annotated code for you to read or run elsewhere; they do not run in this browser.

modules.title: Data engineering foundations
modules.summary: Understand what data engineers do, how data moves from source systems to analysis, where it is stored, and the file formats and processing styles you will meet.
modules.outcome: You can describe the data lifecycle and the engineer's role, tell OLTP from OLAP systems, choose between a warehouse, lake and lakehouse, explain why columnar formats suit analytics, and distinguish batch from streaming and ETL from ELT.
modules.intro: Behind every dashboard is a pipeline that moved data from where it was created to where it can be analysed, and fixed it on the way. Building and running those pipelines reliably is data engineering. This course covers the ideas that hold across tools and clouds: how data is modelled, transformed, tested, scheduled and secured, and it practises them in SQL. This course teaches data engineering with the tool every pipeline shares: SQL. The SQL windows and labs run in your browser on a small online shop's raw tables. Python, Spark, Airflow and Kafka code is shown as annotated listings for you to read or to run in your own environment; it does not run in this browser, and the lessons say so wherever it applies.

topics.title: What data engineers do
topics.html:
A data engineer builds and maintains the systems that collect data, move it, store it, clean it and make it ready for others to use. Their products are reliable datasets and pipelines, not charts or models.

Who does what
RoleMain questionTypical output
Data engineerHow do we get trustworthy data to the people who need it, reliably and at scale?Pipelines, warehouse tables, data quality checks
Data analystWhat happened, and why?Reports, dashboards, ad-hoc analyses
Data scientistWhat will happen, and what should we do?Models, experiments, predictions
Analytics engineerHow do we turn raw tables into clean, documented, tested models for analysis?SQL transformation layers (staging and marts)

Underneath every stage run concerns that decide whether a pipeline is good: security, data management (quality, lineage, governance), orchestration (what runs when), observability (knowing it works), and cost. A pipeline that is fast but untrustworthy, or accurate but unaffordable, is not finished.

Worked example

A day in a data engineer's work

A retailer's analysts say yesterday's revenue looks too low.

  1. Check the pipeline's run history: the order-events load failed at 02:10.
  2. Find the cause: the source system added a column and the loader rejected the file.
  3. Fix the loader, rerun for yesterday without duplicating anything, and add a check that alerts when a load is late.

Answer. The job is as much about reliability and diagnosis as about writing code.

Watch out

Data engineering is not 'moving files around'. It is engineering: tests, monitoring, version control and thought about failure. Treat pipelines like software that other people depend on.

Common mistakes

  • Building pipelines with no monitoring: failures are found by angry users.
  • Treating the data engineer as the owner of the data's meaning: business owners define it, engineers make it reliable.
  • Ignoring cost until the cloud bill arrives.
Try it yourself: Which role mainly builds the pipelines that deliver clean data?

Model answer. The data engineer.

Check what you just learned

1. A data engineer's main product is:
  • A dashboard
  • Reliable pipelines and datasets (correct)
  • A machine learning model
  • A logo

Others build on their datasets.

2. Which is part of the data lifecycle?
  • Compose
  • Decorate
  • Ingest (correct)
  • Print

Ingestion brings data into your systems.
keyPoints: Data engineers build reliable pipelines and datasets; analysts and scientists use them.
The lifecycle is generate, ingest, store, transform, serve, with security, quality, orchestration, observability and cost throughout.
Reliability and diagnosis are central to the job.

topics.title: Where data lives: OLTP, OLAP, warehouses, lakes and lakehouses
topics.html:
Different systems store data for different jobs. The first distinction is between systems that run the business and systems that analyse it.

OLTP and OLAP
OLTP (transactions)OLAP (analytics)
PurposeRun the application: place an order, update a profileAnswer questions across lots of history
QueriesMany small reads and writes of single rowsFewer, large scans and aggregations
DesignNormalised tables, strong consistencyDimensional models, denormalised for reading
ExampleThe shop's order database (MySQL, PostgreSQL)A data warehouse (BigQuery, Snowflake, Redshift, and others)

Running heavy analytics on the live OLTP database slows the shop down, which is why we copy data out to systems built for analysis.

Warehouse, lake and lakehouse
StoreWhat it holdsStrengthsWatch out
Data warehouseStructured, modelled tablesFast SQL, strong governance, easy for analystsLess flexible for raw or unstructured data; cost grows with data and queries
Data lakeFiles of any kind (raw logs, JSON, images) in cheap object storageCheap, flexible, keeps raw dataCan turn into a 'swamp' without structure and governance
LakehouseOpen table formats on lake storage with warehouse-like features (transactions, schemas)One copy of data for SQL, data science and streamingNewer, still maturing; more moving parts

A first look at raw data

Eight raw events for three orders. COUNT(*) counts rows, COUNT(DISTINCT event_id) counts events. The two differ: what does that tell you?

Tables: raw_events. Starting query:

SELECT COUNT(*) AS rows_received,
       COUNT(DISTINCT event_id) AS distinct_events,
       COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) AS orders
FROM raw_events;
Worked example

Why the lake keeps the raw data

A bug in the cleaning logic corrupted two months of results.

  1. Because the raw events are stored unchanged in the lake, you can fix the logic and reprocess them.
  2. If you had only kept the cleaned tables, the original values would be gone.
  3. Keep an untouched raw layer: it is your safety net.

Answer. Cheap storage for raw data buys you the ability to correct mistakes.

Watch out

Cloud product names and features change quickly. Learn the categories and the trade-offs (structured versus flexible, cost versus speed) and check each vendor's current documentation when you choose a tool.

Common mistakes

  • Running analytics queries on the production transactional database.
  • Throwing away raw data after cleaning it.
  • Choosing a platform by its marketing instead of by your workload.
Try it yourself: Why not run a year-long revenue report on the live shop database?

Model answer. Large scans slow the transactional system customers are using; copy data to an analytical store instead.

Check what you just learned

1. OLTP systems are designed for:
  • Large historical scans
  • Dashboards only
  • Image storage
  • Many small reads and writes of single rows (correct)

They run the application.

2. A data lake typically stores:
  • Files of any kind in cheap storage (correct)
  • Only perfectly modelled tables
  • Only dashboards
  • Only passwords

Raw files in object storage.
keyPoints: OLTP runs the business with small reads and writes; OLAP analyses history with large scans.
Warehouses are structured and fast, lakes are cheap and flexible, lakehouses combine them.
Keep an untouched raw layer.

topics.title: File formats: row versus columnar
topics.html:
Data is stored in files, and the format changes how fast and how cheaply you can read it.

Common formats
FormatLayoutGood forNotes
CSVText, one row per lineSimple exchange, small filesNo types; commas and quotes cause trouble; no schema
JSON (and JSON Lines)Text, nested recordsAPIs and events with nested dataVerbose; repeated field names; flexible but loose
AvroBinary, row-oriented, with an embedded schemaStreaming messages, record-at-a-time writesCompact; supports schema evolution
ParquetBinary, columnar, compressedAnalytics on large tablesReads only the columns you ask for; good compression
ORCBinary, columnarAnalytics, especially in Hive-style systemsSimilar benefits to Parquet

In a row-oriented format all the values of one record sit together: great for writing a record or reading a whole row. In a columnar format all the values of one column sit together: great when a query needs three columns out of fifty, because the other forty-seven are never read, and similar values next to each other compress very well.

Worked example

Why columnar wins for analytics

A table has 40 columns and 100 million rows. A report needs order_date and amount.

  1. A row-oriented file must read all 40 columns of every row to find two values.
  2. A columnar file reads only those two columns, about 5% of the data.
  3. Repeated values (the same date, the same status) also compress extremely well, so even those two columns are small.

Answer. Columnar formats are the default for analytics because reports read few columns of many rows.

Watch out

CSV looks harmless but is a common source of silent errors: a comma inside a text field, a date read as text, a leading zero lost from a code. Prefer a typed format (Parquet) for anything beyond a one-off exchange.

Common mistakes

  • Storing large analytical data as CSV.
  • Using a columnar file for single-record updates (write-heavy workloads suit row formats and databases).
  • Forgetting to record the schema of a JSON feed that changes.
Try it yourself: Which format reads only two columns out of fifty cheaply?

Model answer. A columnar format such as Parquet.

Check what you just learned

1. Parquet is:
  • Row-oriented text
  • A columnar binary format (correct)
  • A database
  • A chart

It stores each column together.

2. Why is columnar good for analytics?
  • It removes the schema
  • It is plain text
  • Queries read only the needed columns (correct)
  • It is slower

Most reports touch few columns.
keyPoints: Row-oriented formats (CSV, JSON, Avro) keep a record together; columnar formats (Parquet, ORC) keep a column together.
Columnar files let analytics read few columns of many rows and compress well.
Prefer typed formats over CSV for anything beyond simple exchange.

topics.title: Batch, streaming, ETL and ELT
topics.html:
Two questions shape most pipelines: how often does data move, and where does it get transformed?

Batch and streaming
StyleHow it worksLatencyGood for
BatchProcess a chunk (an hour, a day) at a scheduled timeMinutes to hoursReports, nightly loads, most analytics
Micro-batchProcess small chunks every few seconds or minutesSeconds to minutesNear-real-time dashboards without full streaming complexity
StreamingProcess each event as it arrivesMilliseconds to secondsFraud checks, live monitoring, alerts

Streaming is not 'better'. It is harder to build, test and operate. If a daily number is good enough, batch is simpler, cheaper and more reliable.

ETL and ELT
ETLELT
OrderExtract, transform, then loadExtract, load, then transform
Where transforms runIn a separate processing tool before the warehouseInside the warehouse, usually in SQL
Raw dataOften not kept in the warehouseKept in the warehouse, then modelled in layers
Why it is commonOlder systems with limited warehouse powerModern warehouses are fast and cheap enough to transform in place

The shape of a transformation

Raw events arrive with a duplicate. This query removes the duplicate delivery. It is the kind of step an ELT pipeline runs inside the warehouse.

Tables: raw_events. Starting query:

SELECT DISTINCT event_id, order_id, status, event_ts
FROM raw_events
ORDER BY event_id;
Worked example

Choosing batch or streaming

A shop wants a daily revenue report, and a warning if card payments suddenly fail.

  1. Daily revenue: batch. It runs once after midnight and is easy to rerun.
  2. Payment failure warning: streaming (or micro-batch every minute), because waiting a day defeats the point.
  3. Both can read the same source events; the choice is per use case.

Answer. Match the speed of the pipeline to the speed of the decision.

Watch out

Real-time is expensive in money and in complexity. Ask what decision is made with the data and how fast it must be made before choosing streaming.

Common mistakes

  • Building a streaming pipeline for a daily report.
  • Transforming data before loading it and then losing the raw version.
  • Assuming ETL and ELT are rival religions: many systems use both.
Try it yourself: In ELT, where is most of the transformation done?

Model answer. Inside the warehouse, usually with SQL, after the raw data is loaded.

Check what you just learned

1. ELT stands for:
  • Extract, link, test
  • Edit, load, test
  • Encode, link, transfer
  • Extract, load, transform (correct)

Load first, transform in the warehouse.

2. For a daily report you should usually choose:
  • Batch (correct)
  • Streaming
  • Neither
  • A chart

Batch is simpler and cheaper.

Key terms: flip and sort

Data engineer
Builds reliable pipelines and datasets.
OLTP
Systems that run the business.
OLAP
Systems that analyse history.
Data lake
Cheap storage of raw files of any kind.
Columnar format
Stores each column together (Parquet, ORC).
Batch
Processing chunks on a schedule.
ELT
Load raw data first, transform in the warehouse.
keyPoints: Batch is simple and cheap; micro-batch and streaming trade complexity for lower latency.
ETL transforms before loading; ELT loads raw data first and transforms in the warehouse.
Choose the speed from the decision the data supports.

modules.title: Data modelling for analytics
modules.summary: Model data for reading: normalisation for transactions, then star schemas with facts, dimensions and grain, and slowly changing dimensions that keep history.
modules.outcome: You can explain normal forms, design a star schema, state the grain of a fact table, choose between SCD types 1, 2 and 3, and build a type 2 history with SQL.
modules.intro: Raw data is shaped for the application that produced it. Analysts need it shaped for questions: one clean table of facts, described by a few dimensions, with history kept where it matters. Modelling is the craft of that reshaping, and it decides whether a report is easy to write or impossible. This module teaches the main patterns, with live SQL for the trickiest one: keeping history when a customer changes city.

topics.title: Normalisation: designing for transactions
topics.html:
Transactional systems are normalised: each fact is stored once, in the table where it belongs, so updates are safe and consistent.

The first three normal forms, in plain words
FormRuleFixes
1NFOne value per cell; no repeating groupsA column holding 'Pen, Book, Lamp' becomes one row per item
2NFEvery non-key column depends on the whole keyIn a table keyed by (order, product), a product name belongs in a products table, not here
3NFNon-key columns depend only on the key, not on each otherA customer's city is stored with the customer, not repeated on every order
Worked example

Normalising an orders sheet

A sheet lists order, customer name, customer city, product, product price, quantity on every row.

  1. Customer name and city repeat on every order: move them to a customers table.
  2. Product name and price repeat: move them to a products table.
  3. Orders keep only ids and the quantity, and reference the others by key.

Answer. Change a customer's city once, and every order sees it. That is the point of normalisation.

Normalisation is excellent for writing data safely, but reading it needs many joins. For analytics we usually denormalise on purpose into a shape that is easy to query. That shape is the star schema.

Watch out

Do not denormalise the operational database to make reports easy. Keep the transactional system clean and build the reporting shape in the analytical store.

Common mistakes

  • Storing the same fact in several places in the transactional database.
  • Reporting directly from a heavily normalised schema with a dozen joins.
  • Normalising a warehouse as if it were an application database.
Try it yourself: Why is a customer's city stored in a customers table, not on each order?

Model answer. So it is stored once: changing it in one place updates it for all orders and avoids contradictions.

Check what you just learned

1. Normalisation mainly helps:
  • Fast large scans
  • Safe, consistent updates (correct)
  • Chart design
  • Compression

Each fact lives in one place.

2. For analytics we usually:
  • Normalise further
  • Delete tables
  • Denormalise into a star schema (correct)
  • Use CSV

Reading wants fewer joins.
keyPoints: Normalisation stores each fact once, which makes writes safe.
1NF removes repeating groups, 2NF and 3NF remove partial and transitive dependencies.
Analytics usually denormalises into a star schema.

topics.title: Star schemas: facts, dimensions and grain
topics.html:
A star schema has a central fact table of measurable events (sales, clicks, shipments) joined to dimension tables that describe them (product, customer, date). It is the standard shape for analytics because queries become simple: join the fact to the dimensions you need, group, and aggregate.

Facts and dimensions
Fact tableDimension table
HoldsEvents and numbers (amount, quantity)Descriptions (names, categories, regions)
RowsManyFewer
KeyForeign keys to each dimensionA unique key (often a surrogate key)
ChangesRows are added over timeAttributes may change (see slowly changing dimensions)
Definition

Grain. What one row of a fact table represents, for example 'one sale line' or 'one order per day per product'. Decide and write down the grain first: everything else follows from it, and mixing grains in one table gives wrong totals.

Query a star schema

Join the fact table to a dimension, group and aggregate. Add the customer or date to the grouping, or change the measure.

Tables: sales, products. Starting query:

SELECT p.category, SUM(s.amount) AS revenue
FROM sales s
JOIN products p ON p.product_id = s.product_id
GROUP BY p.category
ORDER BY revenue DESC;

Habits of a good star schema

  • State the grain in words.
  • Surrogate keys: use a meaningless integer key in each dimension instead of a natural key that may change.
  • Conformed dimensions: share one customer or date dimension across fact tables so they can be combined.
  • A date dimension with year, month, week and holiday flags, built once.
  • Degenerate dimensions: an identifier such as an order number can live in the fact table.
  • Keep measures additive where possible (amount), and be careful with ratios (store the parts, compute the ratio).
Watch out

Mixing grains is the classic mistake. Putting an order-level shipping fee on every order-line row means summing the fee multiplies it by the number of lines. Keep each fact at one grain, or split into two facts.

Common mistakes

  • A fact table with an unstated grain.
  • Storing a ratio such as margin % as a column and averaging it.
  • Different customer definitions in different fact tables.
Try it yourself: What is the grain of a table with one row per product sold on each order?

Model answer. One order line (an order and a product).

Check what you just learned

1. The grain of a fact table is:
  • Its file size
  • The number of columns
  • Its colour
  • What one row represents (correct)

It defines what one row is.

2. A fact table typically contains:
  • Events and numeric measures with keys to dimensions (correct)
  • Descriptions only
  • Passwords
  • Charts

Facts are measurable events.
keyPoints: A star schema is a fact table joined to dimensions; queries become join, group, aggregate.
Write the grain first; do not mix grains.
Use surrogate keys, conformed dimensions and a date dimension.

topics.title: Slowly changing dimensions: keeping history
topics.html:
Dimension attributes change: a customer moves city, a product moves category. Reports about the past should usually use the value as it was then. Techniques for this are called slowly changing dimensions (SCDs).

The common types
TypeWhat it doesHistory kept?Use when
Type 1Overwrite the old valueNoCorrections, or when history does not matter
Type 2Add a new row with validity datesYes, fullyHistory matters (analysing sales by the city the customer lived in then)
Type 3Keep the old value in an extra columnOnly the previous valueYou need 'current and previous' only

Type 2 is the one to master. Each change creates a new version of the row, with valid_from, valid_to and often an is_current flag. A fact joins to the version that was valid on the date of the event.

Customer 1 moved from Pune to Mumbai on 10 March 2025
customer_idcityvalid_fromvalid_tois_current
1Pune2025-01-012025-03-100
1Mumbai2025-03-109999-12-311

Build type 2 history from a change log

LEAD looks at the next change for the same customer: that date is when this version stops being valid. The last version has no next change, so we use a far-future date.

Tables: changes. Starting query:

SELECT customer_id, city,
       changed_at AS valid_from,
       COALESCE(
         LEAD(changed_at) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY changed_at),
         '9999-12-31'
       ) AS valid_to
FROM changes
ORDER BY customer_id, changed_at;
Worked example

Joining facts to the version that was valid

Sale 3 on 2025-03-12 belongs to customer 1, who moved on 2025-03-10.

  1. A plain join on customer_id would match both versions and double count.
  2. Add the date condition: sale_date >= valid_from AND sale_date < valid_to.
  3. Only the version valid on that date matches: Mumbai.

Answer. The date range in the join picks exactly one version per sale.

Watch out

Use a half-open range (>= valid_from AND < valid_to) so a date that equals a boundary matches exactly one version. A closed range matches two.

Common mistakes

  • Joining a fact to a type 2 dimension on the key alone, which duplicates rows.
  • Overlapping or gapped validity ranges.
  • Using type 1 when analysts need history.
Try it yourself: Which SCD type keeps full history by adding rows with validity dates?

Model answer. Type 2.

Check what you just learned

1. Which SCD type adds a new row with validity dates?
  • Type 1
  • Type 2 (correct)
  • Type 3
  • None

Type 2 keeps full history.

2. A half-open range is:
  • Any dates
  • <= start and >= end
  • >= start and < end (correct)
  • Only the end

It matches exactly one version.
keyPoints: Type 1 overwrites, type 2 adds a versioned row, type 3 keeps only the previous value.
Type 2 uses valid_from, valid_to and is_current; build it with LEAD.
Join facts on the key and a half-open date range to match one version.

topics.title: Choosing a model: wide tables, partitions and trade-offs
topics.html:
The star schema is a strong default, not the only option. Modern platforms offer other choices, each trading simplicity, flexibility and cost.

Modelling choices
ChoiceWhat it isGood forCost
Star schemaFact plus dimensionsGeneral analytics, BI toolsJoins at query time; modelling effort
One big table (wide table)Facts and dimension attributes flattened togetherSimple, fast dashboardsDuplicated text; harder to change a dimension
Snowflake schemaDimensions normalised furtherSaving storage, complex hierarchiesMore joins; harder to read
Data vaultHubs, links and satellites that keep every source's historyAuditable integration of many sourcesComplex; usually needs a presentation layer on top

Physical design that affects speed and cost

  • Partitioning: split a large table by a column (often date) so a query for one month reads only that partition.
  • Clustering or sorting: order data inside partitions by columns that are often filtered or joined on.
  • Data types: use compact, correct types (dates as dates, not text).
  • Granularity: pre-aggregate (daily instead of per-event) when the detail is not needed.
Worked example

Partitioning by date

A table holds three years of events and most reports ask about the last week.

  1. Partition the table by event date.
  2. A query for the last 7 days reads 7 partitions, not 1,100.
  3. The same query is far faster and cheaper.

Answer. Choose the partition column from how the data is queried, not from how it arrives.

Watch out

There is no perfect model. Start with a clear grain and a simple star schema, measure the real queries, and only then add complexity such as extra aggregates or wide tables.

Common mistakes

  • Partitioning by a column nobody filters on.
  • Too many tiny partitions, which makes files small and queries slow.
  • Premature optimisation before knowing the queries.
Try it yourself: Which column is usually the best candidate to partition event data by?

Model answer. The event date, because most queries filter by time.

Check what you just learned

1. Partitioning a big table by date helps because:
  • It deletes old data
  • It removes the need for SQL
  • It adds colour
  • Queries for a date range read only the matching partitions (correct)

Less data is read.

2. A good first model for analytics is:
  • A simple star schema with a stated grain (correct)
  • Data vault always
  • One CSV
  • No model

Start simple.

Key terms: flip and sort

Normalisation
Storing each fact once.
Star schema
A fact table joined to dimension tables.
Grain
What one row of a fact table represents.
Surrogate key
A meaningless integer key for a dimension row.
SCD type 2
A new versioned row with validity dates.
Conformed dimension
A dimension shared by several fact tables.
Partitioning
Splitting a table by a column to read less.
keyPoints: Star schemas are the default; wide tables, snowflakes and data vault serve special needs.
Partition by how data is queried (often date) and cluster by common filters.
Start simple and measure.

modules.title: SQL transformations and data quality
modules.summary: Turn raw tables into trusted ones in layers, remove duplicates, keep the latest record, load incrementally, and test the data with SQL.
modules.outcome: You can structure raw, staging and mart layers, deduplicate and find the latest record with window functions, describe incremental and idempotent loads, and write SQL data-quality checks.
modules.intro: Most of a data engineer's day-to-day work is SQL that cleans and reshapes data. Done well, it is organised in layers, repeatable, and tested, so a failure is caught by a check rather than by an executive. This module teaches those habits and practises the core techniques on a raw order-event log that has exactly the problems real logs have: duplicates, out-of-order events, and bad values.

topics.title: Layers: raw, staging and marts
topics.html:
A good pipeline does not transform data in one giant step. It moves data through layers, each with one job, so problems are easy to find and fix.

A common layering
LayerAlso calledWhat it holdsRules
RawBronze, landingData exactly as receivedNever change it; keep load time and source
StagingSilver, cleanedTyped, deduplicated, renamed, one table per sourceNo business logic; fix technical problems
MartsGold, presentationBusiness-ready models (star schemas, aggregates)Business definitions live here; documented and tested

Why layers help

  • Reprocess from raw after a bug without going back to the source.
  • Find where a number went wrong by checking each layer.
  • Reuse a clean staging table in many marts.
  • Separate technical cleaning from business definitions.
  • Test each layer with checks suited to it.
Worked example

A wrong total traced through layers

The revenue mart shows 12% too much.

  1. Raw order events: counts match the source.
  2. Staging: a duplicate-delivery issue is found; staging still holds 15 duplicate events.
  3. Fix the staging dedupe; rebuild the mart. The total is right.

Answer. Layers turn 'the number is wrong' into 'the problem is in this step'.

Watch out

Do not put business logic (what counts as revenue) in staging, and do not clean raw data in place. Each layer has one job; mixing jobs makes every layer hard to trust.

Common mistakes

  • Overwriting raw data after cleaning it.
  • Staging tables that quietly drop rows with no record of why.
  • Business rules scattered across many layers.
Try it yourself: Which layer should hold data exactly as received?

Model answer. Raw (bronze/landing).

Check what you just learned

1. Raw data should be:
  • Cleaned in place
  • Kept exactly as received (correct)
  • Deleted after use
  • Duplicated by hand

Raw is your safety net.

2. Business definitions such as revenue belong in:
  • Raw
  • The source
  • Marts (correct)
  • Emails

Marts hold business logic.
keyPoints: Raw, staging and mart layers each have one job.
Never change raw data; do technical cleaning in staging; put business logic in marts.
Layers make problems traceable and rebuilds possible.

topics.title: Deduplicating and finding the latest record
topics.html:
Event logs and change feeds nearly always contain duplicates (the same message delivered twice) and history (several rows per entity). Two patterns handle most cases.

Two patterns
ProblemPattern
The same event delivered more than once (identical rows)SELECT DISTINCT ..., or number rows per event id and keep the first
Several records per entity; you want the latestROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY entity ORDER BY timestamp DESC, id DESC) and keep rn = 1

Latest status per order

First remove the duplicate delivery, then keep the newest event for each order. Order 101 ends 'shipped', 102 'cancelled', 103 'paid'.

Tables: raw_events. Starting query:

SELECT order_id, status
FROM (
  SELECT order_id, status,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
           PARTITION BY order_id
           ORDER BY event_ts DESC, event_id DESC
         ) AS rn
  FROM (SELECT DISTINCT * FROM raw_events) d
) t
WHERE rn = 1
ORDER BY order_id;

Notice the tie-breaker event_id DESC in the ORDER BY. If two events for an order share a timestamp, without it the 'latest' row could change from run to run. A deterministic ordering makes the result repeatable.

Worked example

Late and out-of-order events

An order's 'paid' event arrives after its 'shipped' event because of a network delay.

  1. Do not rely on arrival order: use the event's own timestamp.
  2. The newest by timestamp wins even if it arrived first.
  3. A late event can later correct earlier results: the pipeline must be able to reprocess.

Answer. Order by when it happened, not when it arrived, and expect late data.

Watch out

DISTINCT * removes only rows that are identical in every column. If duplicates differ in a load timestamp or id column, they will survive. Decide which columns define 'the same event' and dedupe on those.

Common mistakes

  • Keeping 'the first row' without an ORDER BY: the result is arbitrary.
  • Deduplicating on all columns when a load-time column differs.
  • Ignoring that an old record can arrive late.
Try it yourself: Which window function and filter keep only the newest row per order?

Model answer. ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY order_id ORDER BY event_ts DESC) and WHERE rn = 1.

Check what you just learned

1. ROW_NUMBER() ... rn = 1 with ORDER BY event_ts DESC keeps:
  • The oldest row
  • A random column
  • All rows
  • The newest row per partition (correct)

Descending puts the newest first.

2. Why add a tie-breaker to the ORDER BY?
  • So the result is repeatable when timestamps tie (correct)
  • To change the colour
  • To add rows
  • It is required by SQL

Otherwise ties are broken arbitrarily.
keyPoints: DISTINCT removes identical duplicate deliveries; ROW_NUMBER with rn = 1 keeps the latest record per entity.
Add a tie-breaker so the result is deterministic.
Order by event time, not arrival time, and expect late data.

topics.title: Incremental loads and idempotency
topics.html:
Reprocessing the whole history every night does not scale. An incremental load processes only what is new or changed since the last run, tracked by a watermark (for example, the latest event timestamp already loaded).

Definition

Idempotent. An operation that gives the same result however many times you run it. An idempotent pipeline can be safely retried or re-run for a past day without creating duplicates or double counting. This is the most important property of a reliable pipeline.

Only the new rows

Change the watermark and see how many events qualify. A real pipeline stores this value and moves it forward after each successful run.

Tables: raw_events. Starting query:

SELECT COUNT(*) AS new_events,
       MAX(event_ts) AS new_watermark
FROM raw_events
WHERE event_ts > '2025-03-01 10:00';
Making a load idempotent
TechniqueHow it helps
Merge (upsert) on a keyA rerun updates rows instead of inserting copies
Replace a whole partitionRe-running a day deletes and rewrites that day only
Deterministic transformationsThe same input always gives the same output (no random ids or 'now()')
Update the watermark lastA failed run does not skip data
Watch out

Use the event's time, not 'now', in transformations. A job that uses the current time gives different answers when re-run for yesterday, which breaks backfills. Pass the date being processed in as a parameter.

Common mistakes

  • Inserting without checking for existing rows, so retries duplicate data.
  • Moving the watermark before the load has succeeded, losing rows on failure.
  • Using the current date inside a daily job.
Try it yourself: Why must a pipeline be idempotent?

Model answer. So it can be retried or re-run for a past period without creating duplicates or wrong totals.

Check what you just learned

1. An idempotent job:
  • Gives different results each run
  • Gives the same result however many times it runs (correct)
  • Can only run once
  • Needs no schedule

Safe to retry.

2. The watermark should be updated:
  • Before the load
  • Never
  • After the load succeeds (correct)
  • At random

Otherwise a failure skips data.
keyPoints: Incremental loads process only data newer than a watermark.
Idempotent pipelines can be re-run safely: use merge, partition replacement and deterministic logic.
Pass the processing date as a parameter and update the watermark last.

topics.title: Testing data with SQL
topics.html:
Data can be wrong without any code failing: a null where there should be a value, a duplicated key, an amount below zero. Data quality tests are queries that look for these problems and fail the pipeline (or alert) when they find some.

The core tests
TestWhat it checksSQL idea
Not nullA required column has a valueCOUNT(*) - COUNT(col)
UniqueA key appears onceCOUNT(*) - COUNT(DISTINCT key)
Accepted valuesA column holds only allowed valuesWHERE status NOT IN (...)
Relationships (referential integrity)Every foreign key has a parentA LEFT JOIN to the parent where the parent is NULL
RangeValues are sensibleWHERE amount < 0
FreshnessData is not staleMAX(loaded_at) compared with now
Row countThe volume is plausibleCompare today's count with the usual range

One query, several tests

Each column counts one kind of problem in a small messy table. A healthy table returns zeros. Add a test for another rule.

Tables: orders_raw, known_customers. Starting query:

SELECT COUNT(*) - COUNT(customer_id) AS null_customers,
       COUNT(*) - COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) AS duplicate_orders,
       SUM(CASE WHEN amount < 0 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS negative_amounts,
       SUM(CASE WHEN status NOT IN ('paid','shipped','cancelled') THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS bad_status
FROM orders_raw;

Orphan rows (a relationships test)

Which orders refer to a customer that does not exist? A LEFT JOIN to the parent, keeping the unmatched rows, finds them.

Tables: orders_raw, known_customers. Starting query:

SELECT o.order_id, o.customer_id
FROM orders_raw o
LEFT JOIN known_customers k
  ON k.customer_id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.customer_id IS NOT NULL
  AND k.customer_id IS NULL;

How to use tests well

  • Run tests after each layer, at the point where the property should hold.
  • Decide per test: fail the pipeline (a broken key) or warn (a small drift in volume).
  • Test the things that would hurt: keys, amounts, dates, counts.
  • Keep failing rows (or a sample) in a table so you can investigate.
  • Add a test for every bug you fix, so it cannot return.
Watch out

A test that never fails may not be testing anything. Occasionally run it on deliberately bad data to confirm it catches the problem.

Common mistakes

  • No tests, so errors are found by users.
  • Tests that only count rows, not content.
  • Alerting on every small issue until nobody reads the alerts.
Try it yourself: Write the SQL idea for a 'unique key' test.

Model answer. COUNT(*) - COUNT(DISTINCT key) should be zero.

Check what you just learned

1. A 'relationships' test finds:
  • Duplicate keys
  • Null amounts
  • Slow queries
  • Foreign keys with no matching parent row (correct)

Orphans reference a missing parent.

2. A healthy quality query returns:
  • Zeros (correct)
  • Large numbers
  • Text
  • Nothing

Each count is the number of violations.

Key terms: flip and sort

Raw / staging / mart
Layers of increasing cleanliness and meaning.
Deduplicate
Remove repeated records.
Watermark
The progress marker for incremental loads.
Idempotent
Same result however many times it runs.
Upsert / merge
Insert new rows and update existing ones by key.
Data quality test
A query that counts violations.
Referential integrity
Every foreign key has a parent.
keyPoints: Data quality tests are queries that count violations: not null, unique, accepted values, relationships, range, freshness, volume.
Run them after each layer and decide whether a failure stops the pipeline.
Add a test for every bug fixed.

modules.title: Pipelines, orchestration and reliability
modules.summary: Design pipelines that can fail safely and be rerun, schedule them as dependency graphs, and keep them observable and tested.
modules.outcome: You can describe the properties of a reliable pipeline, read and explain a DAG, handle retries and backfills, and list the monitoring and testing a production pipeline needs.
modules.intro: Writing a query that works once is the easy part. A pipeline has to run every day, in the right order, survive failures, and tell you when something is wrong. This module is about that: designing for failure, scheduling with orchestration (usually DAGs), and the testing and monitoring habits that let you sleep. This course teaches data engineering with the tool every pipeline shares: SQL. The SQL windows and labs run in your browser on a small online shop's raw tables. Python, Spark, Airflow and Kafka code is shown as annotated listings for you to read or to run in your own environment; it does not run in this browser, and the lessons say so wherever it applies.

topics.title: Designing a reliable pipeline
topics.html:
Reliable pipelines share a small set of design habits.

Principles of a reliable pipeline

  • Idempotent: re-running for the same period gives the same result, with no duplicates.
  • Deterministic: the same inputs give the same outputs. Avoid 'now()' and random values inside transformations.
  • Atomic: a step either completes fully or not at all, so a crash leaves no half-written data. (Write to a temporary location and swap, or use transactions.)
  • Small, single-purpose steps: easier to test, retry and understand than one giant job.
  • Explicit dependencies: a step runs only after the steps it needs have succeeded.
  • Parameterised by date: every run is told which period to process, so backfills are easy.
  • Observable: it logs what it did and how many rows it handled.
Worked example

Atomic writes

A job writes 5 million rows into the daily revenue table and crashes at row 3 million.

  1. Without atomicity, the table now holds half a day: dashboards show wrong totals and a rerun duplicates the first half.
  2. With an atomic write, the job builds the result in a temporary table and swaps it in at the end.
  3. A crash leaves the old, complete table in place.

Answer. A pipeline should never leave data half-written.

Definition

Data contract. An agreement between the team that produces data and the team that consumes it: which columns, types, meanings and freshness to expect. A change that breaks the contract (a renamed column, a new unit) is announced and versioned instead of discovered when a pipeline fails.

Watch out

The most common outage is not a code bug: it is a change in the source that nobody told you about. Validate the schema on ingestion and fail loudly, with a clear message, when it changes.

Common mistakes

  • Pipelines that append blindly and duplicate on retry.
  • Jobs that read the current time inside the logic.
  • One enormous script that does everything and cannot be rerun in parts.
Try it yourself: Why should a pipeline take the date to process as a parameter?

Model answer. So a past period can be re-run (a backfill) and the logic does not depend on when it happens to run.

Check what you just learned

1. An atomic write means:
  • It is fast
  • It completes fully or not at all (correct)
  • It uses colour
  • It runs twice

A crash leaves no partial data.

2. A data contract describes:
  • A legal case
  • A chart
  • What data a producer promises to consumers (correct)
  • A password

Columns, types, meanings and freshness.
keyPoints: Reliable pipelines are idempotent, deterministic, atomic, small-stepped, parameterised by date and observable.
Data contracts make source changes visible before they break pipelines.
Validate schemas on ingestion and fail loudly.

topics.title: Orchestration: DAGs, schedules, retries and backfills
topics.html:
An orchestrator runs your pipeline's steps in the right order, on a schedule, retries failures and records what happened. Most describe a pipeline as a DAG (directed acyclic graph): tasks as nodes, dependencies as arrows, with no cycles.

Orchestration concepts
ConceptMeaning
TaskOne unit of work (run a query, call an API)
DependencyTask B starts only after task A succeeds
ScheduleWhen the DAG runs: hourly, daily at 02:00
RetryRe-run a failed task, usually with a delay, up to a limit
BackfillRun the DAG for past periods (after a fix or a new pipeline)
SensorA task that waits for something (a file, a table, another DAG)
AlertingNotify people when a task fails or runs too long
Worked example

Reading the DAG

The code above.

  1. Two tasks: extract and transform.
  2. t1 >> t2 means transform depends on extract.
  3. It runs daily, passes the date being processed (ds) to each task, and retries a failing task up to three times, five minutes apart.

Answer. Other orchestrators (Dagster, Prefect, cloud schedulers) express the same ideas with different syntax.

Watch out

Backfills multiply load. Re-running 400 past days at once can overwhelm the source system or the warehouse. Limit concurrency, and make sure each run is idempotent so partial reruns are safe.

Common mistakes

  • Hard-coding dates so a backfill is impossible.
  • Retrying forever with no alert.
  • A dependency cycle (A needs B needs A): a graph must be acyclic.
Try it yourself: What does t1 >> t2 mean in an Airflow DAG?

Model answer. Task t2 runs only after task t1 has succeeded.

Check what you just learned

1. DAG stands for:
  • Direct append group
  • Data access gateway
  • Daily automated grid
  • Directed acyclic graph (correct)

A graph with arrows and no cycles.

2. A backfill is:
  • Running a pipeline for past periods (correct)
  • A new chart
  • A type of join
  • A password reset

It fills in history.
keyPoints: A DAG lists tasks and dependencies with no cycles; an orchestrator schedules, retries and records runs.
Pass the processing date to tasks so backfills work.
Limit concurrency on backfills and alert on failures.

topics.title: Monitoring, alerting and failure handling
topics.html:
A pipeline you cannot see is a pipeline you cannot trust. Observability means you can tell, at any time, whether it is working and why not.

What to watch
SignalExampleWhy it matters
Run statusTask failed or succeededThe basic signal
DurationToday's load took 40 minutes instead of 8A leading indicator of trouble
FreshnessThe orders table was last updated 30 hours agoWhat users actually experience
VolumeRow count fell 90% from yesterdayCatches silent partial loads
QualityDuplicate keys appearedWrong data with no error
CostWarehouse spend doubled this weekFinds runaway queries

A good alerting policy

  • Alert on user-visible problems (stale data, failed quality tests), not on every internal hiccup.
  • Send alerts to a channel someone owns, with a link to the run and logs.
  • Define a service level (for example 'the revenue table is ready by 07:00 on 99% of days') and alert when it is at risk.
  • Write a runbook: the steps to diagnose and fix the common failures.
  • After an incident, write down the cause and add a check or alert so it cannot repeat silently.
Worked example

A silent failure caught by a volume check

The orders load 'succeeded', but today's table has 3,000 rows against a usual 90,000.

  1. The source API returned only the first page because of a timeout, and the loader did not notice.
  2. A volume check (today's rows within 50% of the 7-day average) failed the run.
  3. The team fixed the pagination and reran the day.

Answer. Success status is not the same as correct data: monitor volume and quality too.

Watch out

Alert fatigue is real. If people receive fifty alerts a day, they stop reading them and miss the one that matters. Alert on what needs action.

Common mistakes

  • Treating 'the job exited with status 0' as proof of correct data.
  • Alerts that go to an email nobody reads.
  • No runbook, so the fix depends on one person's memory.
Try it yourself: Why monitor row counts as well as run status?

Model answer. A job can finish without errors but load only part of the data; a volume check catches that silent failure.

Check what you just learned

1. A volume check catches:
  • Slow typing
  • Silent partial loads (correct)
  • Colour problems
  • Typos in titles

Row counts reveal missing data.

2. A runbook is:
  • A race plan
  • A database
  • Steps to diagnose and fix common failures (correct)
  • A schedule

It makes fixes repeatable.
keyPoints: Watch run status, duration, freshness, volume, quality and cost.
Alert on user-visible problems, to an owned channel, with a runbook.
A successful run is not proof of correct data: check volume and quality.

topics.title: Testing, version control and deployment of data pipelines
topics.html:
Data pipelines are software, so they deserve software practices.

Kinds of tests
TestWhat it checksExample
Unit testOne transformation on tiny, known inputA dedupe function keeps the latest of two duplicate rows
Data testProperties of real dataNo null keys; no negative amounts
Integration testSteps working togetherExtract, load and transform on a small sample end to end
Regression testA fixed bug stays fixedThe case that broke production is now a test
ReconciliationTotals agree between systemsWarehouse revenue equals the finance system's

Good engineering habits

  • Version control (Git) for all pipeline code and SQL, with code review.
  • Separate environments: development, test and production, with different data and permissions.
  • Continuous integration: tests run automatically on every change.
  • Small, reviewable changes, deployed often.
  • Configuration outside code: connection strings and settings in configuration or a secrets manager, never in the repository.
  • Documentation next to the code: what each model is and what its columns mean.
Worked example

A unit test for a transformation

A staging query keeps the latest status per order.

  1. Create three tiny test rows: two for order 1 (older 'paid', newer 'shipped') and one for order 2.
  2. Run the transformation on them.
  3. Assert that the result has exactly two rows and order 1's status is 'shipped'.

Answer. A tiny, deterministic input makes a bug in the logic obvious in seconds.

Tools such as dbt have made this style common for SQL transformations: models are SQL files in version control, tests (not null, unique, accepted values, relationships) are declared beside them, and documentation is generated from the code. The ideas apply whether or not you use any particular tool.

Watch out

Never test only in production. A change that has not run on test data first can corrupt the tables that executives read. Use a separate environment and promote changes after they pass.

Common mistakes

  • Pipelines edited directly on the production server.
  • Credentials committed to the repository.
  • A growing set of untested SQL files.
Try it yourself: Why keep connection passwords out of the code repository?

Model answer. Repositories are widely accessible and permanent; secrets belong in a secrets manager or protected configuration.

Check what you just learned

1. A unit test uses:
  • The whole production database
  • No data
  • A dashboard
  • Tiny, known input and an expected output (correct)

It checks one transformation precisely.

2. Credentials should be stored in:
  • A secrets manager or protected configuration (correct)
  • The repository
  • A chat message
  • A comment

Never commit secrets.

Key terms: flip and sort

Idempotent
Same result on every rerun.
Atomic
All or nothing.
DAG
Tasks and dependencies with no cycles.
Backfill
Running a pipeline for past periods.
Observability
Being able to see whether the pipeline works.
Runbook
Written steps for diagnosing and fixing failures.
Data contract
An agreement on what data is delivered.
keyPoints: Test transformations (unit), real data (data tests), the whole flow (integration) and fixed bugs (regression).
Use version control, separate environments, CI and small reviewed changes.
Keep secrets and configuration out of code.

modules.title: Big data and streaming
modules.summary: Understand how work is split across many machines, how files and partitions are laid out for speed, and how streaming systems handle events as they arrive.
modules.outcome: You can explain partitioning and shuffles, read a Spark DataFrame example, lay out files in a lake sensibly, describe topics, partitions and consumer groups, and explain windows, late data and delivery guarantees.
modules.intro: When data no longer fits on one machine, or arrives faster than one machine can handle, the work is split across many. This module explains how that works without tying you to one product: the ideas of partitioning, shuffling and skew; how files should be laid out in a lake; and how streaming systems treat an endless flow of events. The code is shown for reading, and the SQL window lets you practise the main streaming idea, windowed aggregation, on a small table. This course teaches data engineering with the tool every pipeline shares: SQL. The SQL windows and labs run in your browser on a small online shop's raw tables. Python, Spark, Airflow and Kafka code is shown as annotated listings for you to read or to run in your own environment; it does not run in this browser, and the lessons say so wherever it applies.

topics.title: Distributed processing: partitions, shuffles and Spark
topics.html:
The core idea of big-data processing is simple: split the data into partitions, process each partition on a different machine in parallel, then combine the results. Systems such as Apache Spark do this for you.

Key terms
TermMeaning
PartitionA slice of the data processed by one task
ClusterSeveral machines working together
TransformationA step that describes a computation (filter, join, group)
ActionA step that triggers the work and returns a result or writes data
ShuffleMoving data between machines so rows with the same key end up together (needed for joins and group-bys)
SkewOne partition far larger than the others, so one machine does most of the work
Worked example

Reading the example

The listing above.

  1. where and groupBy are transformations: nothing runs yet.
  2. write is an action: Spark now plans the work, splits it over partitions, shuffles rows so each order_date's rows meet, sums them and writes one folder per date.
  3. The same logic in SQL is SELECT order_date, SUM(amount) FROM orders WHERE status = 'delivered' GROUP BY order_date.

Answer. Spark and SQL warehouses solve the same problem; Spark gives you code-level control and works on files in a lake.

Watch out

Shuffles are the expensive part. Joins and group-bys move data across the network. Filtering early, selecting only needed columns and avoiding unnecessary joins make jobs far cheaper than adding machines.

Do you need Spark?

  • If your data fits comfortably in a warehouse or even one machine, use SQL on a warehouse or a single-node tool: it is simpler.
  • Reach for a distributed engine when data is too large for one machine, when you process files in a lake at scale, or when you need custom code beyond SQL.
  • Choose by the workload and team skills, not by fashion.

Common mistakes

  • Using a cluster for data that fits on a laptop.
  • Joining two huge tables without thinking about the shuffle.
  • Ignoring skew: one hot key making a job crawl.
Try it yourself: What is a shuffle, and why is it costly?

Model answer. Moving rows across machines so rows with the same key meet; it uses the network and disk, so it is slow compared with local work.

Check what you just learned

1. A partition is:
  • A database user
  • A slice of the data processed by one task (correct)
  • A chart
  • A file extension

Parallelism comes from partitions.

2. Which is usually the most expensive step?
  • A filter on one column
  • Naming a column
  • A shuffle across machines (correct)
  • Reading a header

It moves data over the network.
keyPoints: Distributed engines split data into partitions processed in parallel, then combine results.
Transformations describe work; an action triggers it; shuffles (for joins and group-bys) are the costly step.
Use a distributed engine only when the data or workload needs it.

topics.title: File layout in a lake: partitions, small files and pruning
topics.html:
In a data lake, how files are laid out decides how fast and cheap queries are.

Layout decisions
DecisionGood practiceBad practice
Partition columnA column queries filter on (usually a date), with moderate cardinalityA column with millions of values (a user id), or one nobody filters
Partition countThousands at most, each with reasonably large filesMillions of tiny folders
File sizeRoughly 128 MB to 1 GB per file (a rule of thumb that varies by engine)Thousands of kilobyte-sized files
FormatColumnar (Parquet) with compressionUncompressed CSV or JSON
Folder structuretable/year=2025/month=03/day=01/part-0001.parquetFiles dumped in one folder
Worked example

The small-files problem

A streaming job writes a new file every minute into each of 500 partitions.

  1. After a day there are 700,000 tiny files.
  2. Listing and opening them dominates the query time; metadata overhead swamps the actual data.
  3. A compaction job merges them into a few large files nightly, and queries become much faster.

Answer. Many small files are a classic data-lake performance problem; compact them.

Watch out

Over-partitioning is as bad as under-partitioning. Partition by something with a sensible number of values, and check file sizes.

Common mistakes

  • Partitioning by a high-cardinality column.
  • Never compacting streaming output.
  • Mixing file formats in one table.
Try it yourself: What does partition pruning do?

Model answer. Lets the engine skip whole partitions that cannot match the query's filter, reading far less data.

Check what you just learned

1. A good partition column is usually:
  • A user id
  • A password
  • A free-text note
  • The event date (correct)

Queries commonly filter by date.

2. The small-files problem is:
  • Too many tiny files slowing queries (correct)
  • Files that are too large
  • Missing colours
  • A security setting

Metadata overhead dominates.
keyPoints: Partition by a filtered, moderate-cardinality column (often date); keep files reasonably large; use Parquet.
Partition pruning skips irrelevant partitions.
Compact small files regularly.

topics.title: Streaming: events, logs, topics and partitions
topics.html:
A streaming system treats data as an endless flow of events (a click, a payment, a sensor reading) and processes them as they arrive. Most streaming platforms are built around a distributed log: an append-only record of events that many consumers can read independently.

The vocabulary (Apache Kafka as the example)
TermMeaning
ProducerAn application that writes events
TopicA named stream of events, such as payments
PartitionA topic is split into partitions for scale; order is guaranteed only within a partition
KeyEvents with the same key (for example an order id) go to the same partition, so their order is kept
OffsetAn event's position in a partition
Consumer groupConsumers sharing the work: each partition is read by one consumer in the group
RetentionHow long events are kept, so slow or new consumers can replay
Delivery guarantees
GuaranteeMeaningCost
At most onceAn event is processed zero or one time; it may be lostSimple, can lose data
At least onceAn event is processed one or more times; it may be repeatedCommon; consumers must tolerate duplicates
Exactly onceEach event's effect is applied onceAchieved by transactions or, more commonly, idempotent processing

In practice, make consumers idempotent (use the event id to ignore a repeat) and accept at-least-once delivery. That is the streaming version of the idempotent batch load.

Worked example

Why order needs a key

Events for order 101 (created, paid, shipped) go to a topic with three partitions.

  1. With no key, events are spread across partitions, and a consumer may see 'shipped' before 'paid'.
  2. With the order id as the key, all of order 101's events go to the same partition, in order.
  3. Order is guaranteed per key, not across the whole topic.

Answer. Choose the key so that events that must stay in order share it.

Watch out

Streaming systems need monitoring of consumer lag (how far behind the consumer is). A growing lag means data is arriving faster than it is processed: users see stale results even though nothing 'failed'.

Common mistakes

  • Assuming events arrive exactly once and in order.
  • Choosing a key with a few hot values, overloading one partition.
  • Forgetting retention: a consumer that is down longer than retention loses events.
Try it yourself: Why make a stream consumer idempotent?

Model answer. Delivery is often at least once, so the same event can arrive twice; idempotent processing makes that harmless.

Check what you just learned

1. Order is guaranteed:
  • Across the whole topic
  • Within a partition (correct)
  • Never
  • Only for numbers

Use a key to keep related events in one partition.

2. At-least-once delivery means:
  • Events are always lost
  • Events are never repeated
  • Events may be repeated (correct)
  • No events

Duplicates are possible.
keyPoints: Streaming platforms keep an append-only log of events in topics split into partitions; order is guaranteed within a partition.
Keys keep related events together and ordered; consumer groups share the work.
Expect at-least-once delivery and make consumers idempotent.

topics.title: Windows, late data and choosing an architecture
topics.html:
Because a stream never ends, aggregations are computed over windows: slices of time.

Window types
WindowShapeExample
TumblingFixed-size, non-overlappingOrders per 10 minutes
Sliding (hopping)Fixed-size, overlappingA 1-hour average, updated every 5 minutes
SessionGrouped by activity with a gap timeoutA user's visit, ended after 30 minutes of inactivity

Tumbling windows in SQL

Seven visits grouped into 10-minute tumbling windows. Streaming systems do the same continuously. Change 10 to 5 for finer windows.

Tables: visits. Starting query:

SELECT SUBSTR(visit_ts, 1, 13) AS hour,
       FLOOR(CAST(SUBSTR(visit_ts, 15, 2) AS INTEGER) / 10) * 10 AS minute_window,
       COUNT(*) AS visits
FROM visits
GROUP BY 1, 2
ORDER BY 1, 2;
Definition

Event time and processing time. Event time is when something happened; processing time is when the system sees it. They differ when data is delayed. Windows should normally use event time, and the system uses a watermark (a promise that events older than some point have probably all arrived) to decide when a window can be closed.

Worked example

Late data

A phone buys something at 10:09 but is offline and the event arrives at 10:23.

  1. Using processing time, the purchase lands in the 10:20 window: wrong.
  2. Using event time, it belongs in the 10:00 window.
  3. The 10:00 window must stay open (or be corrected) until the watermark says late events are unlikely.

Answer. Late data forces a trade-off between waiting longer (accurate, delayed) and answering sooner (fast, may need correcting).

Choosing an architecture
NeedReasonable choice
A daily reportBatch: a scheduled SQL job
A dashboard fresh to the minuteMicro-batch or incremental loads every few minutes
Alert within seconds of a payment fraud patternStreaming with event-time windows
Both history and live viewBatch for history; streaming for recent data; reconcile or unify them (the Lambda and Kappa ideas)
Watch out

Each step toward real time adds cost and operational burden. Make sure a faster answer would change a decision.

Common mistakes

  • Windowing on processing time and misplacing late events.
  • Closing windows too early and dropping late data.
  • Building two separate pipelines for the same metric with different numbers.
Try it yourself: Which window type groups a user's activity by gaps of inactivity?

Model answer. A session window.

Check what you just learned

1. A tumbling window is:
  • Overlapping
  • A file format
  • Based on gaps
  • Fixed-size and non-overlapping (correct)

Each event is in exactly one window.

2. Event time is:
  • When the event actually happened (correct)
  • When the system saw the event
  • The server clock
  • The file name

Use it for correct windows.

Key terms: flip and sort

Partition
A slice of data processed in parallel.
Shuffle
Moving rows between machines by key.
Partition pruning
Skipping partitions that cannot match.
Topic
A named stream of events.
Offset
An event's position in a partition.
Tumbling window
Fixed, non-overlapping time slices.
Watermark
A promise about how late events can be.
keyPoints: Windows (tumbling, sliding, session) aggregate a never-ending stream.
Use event time and watermarks to handle late data.
Choose batch, micro-batch or streaming from how fast the decision must be made.

modules.title: Governance, security, cost and practice
modules.summary: Keep data trustworthy and safe: quality management, lineage, access control, privacy, cost control and writing a pipeline design document.
modules.outcome: You can describe quality dimensions and lineage, apply least privilege and masking to personal data, name the privacy laws involved at a high level, control cost, and write a short pipeline design document.
modules.intro: A pipeline that produces correct numbers can still be a liability if it exposes personal data, costs more than the value it creates, or cannot be explained when an auditor asks where a number came from. This final module covers the responsibilities around the pipelines: quality, lineage, security, privacy, cost and communication. It ends with the final project: a transformation built on the shop's raw tables, and a design document for the pipeline. This is general guidance, not legal advice.

topics.title: Data quality, lineage and ownership
topics.html:
Data quality is not one thing. It has several dimensions, and different data needs different ones.

Dimensions of data quality
DimensionQuestionExample check
CompletenessIs anything missing?Share of customers with a city
ValidityDoes it follow the rules?Amounts are not negative; status is one of the allowed values
UniquenessIs anything repeated?One row per order id
ConsistencyDo systems agree?Warehouse revenue equals the finance system's
TimelinessIs it current?The table was updated by 07:00
AccuracyIs it true?Spot-check against the source or a physical count

Lineage records where a dataset came from and what depends on it: source, transformations, downstream tables and reports. It answers 'where does this number come from?' and, before a change, 'what will break?'. Ownership gives every dataset a named owner who is accountable for its meaning and quality.

Habits that keep data trusted

  • Assign an owner to each important dataset.
  • Publish a catalog: what each table is, its columns, owner, freshness and quality status.
  • Track lineage, automatically where tools allow.
  • Use data contracts with source teams.
  • Measure and publish quality scores and freshness.
  • Make fixing quality issues part of normal work, with a way to report problems.
Worked example

Impact analysis

A source team plans to rename the amount column.

  1. Lineage shows 14 staging models and 6 dashboards depend on it.
  2. The change is announced, versioned and rolled out with both names for a period.
  3. No dashboard breaks.

Answer. Lineage turns an unknown risk into a checklist.

Watch out

Quality is a shared responsibility. If only the engineer cares, problems are found late. Give business owners the means to see and report quality.

Common mistakes

  • No owner, so nobody fixes a known problem.
  • Documentation written once and never updated.
  • Discovering dependencies only after something breaks.
Try it yourself: What question does lineage answer before changing a column?

Model answer. What downstream tables and reports depend on it, and so what will break.

Check what you just learned

1. Lineage helps you:
  • Choose colours
  • See what depends on a dataset (correct)
  • Compress files
  • Rename people

Impact analysis.

2. Uniqueness checks:
  • Whether it is accurate
  • Whether data is fresh
  • Whether anything is repeated (correct)
  • File size

A key should appear once.
keyPoints: Quality has dimensions: completeness, validity, uniqueness, consistency, timeliness, accuracy.
Lineage shows sources and dependents; ownership gives accountability.
Catalogs, contracts and published quality status keep data trusted.

topics.title: Security and privacy
topics.html:
Data engineers handle some of the most sensitive information an organisation holds. Security and privacy are part of the design from the start.

Core protections
PracticeWhat it does
Least privilegeEach person and service gets only the access needed for their job
Role-based access controlPermissions are granted to roles, and people are assigned roles
Encryption in transit and at restData is unreadable if intercepted or if storage is stolen
Secrets managementPasswords and keys live in a secrets manager, not in code
Masking and pseudonymisationReplace identifying values (a name, a phone number) with masked or tokenised ones for people who do not need the real value
Audit loggingRecord who accessed what, and when
Retention and deletionKeep personal data only as long as needed, and delete it on schedule or on request

Handling personal data (PII)

  • Minimise: do not collect or copy more than you need.
  • Separate: keep identifiers apart from behavioural data where you can, joined only for those who need it.
  • Mask by default in analytical layers; allow the real value only to authorised roles.
  • Know where it is: tag columns that hold personal data.
  • Plan for deletion: be able to find and remove one person's data across layers and backups.

Laws such as India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 and the EU's GDPR set rules on consent, purpose, security, retention and people's rights over their data. The details depend on where you operate and whose data you hold, so involve your legal and privacy teams, and follow your organisation's policy. The engineering habits above support compliance, but a pipeline is not compliant just because it is encrypted.

Worked example

Masking in the analytical layer

Analysts need to count customers by city, not to see their phone numbers.

  1. The staging layer keeps the phone number, readable only by a small engineering role.
  2. The mart exposes a hashed customer id and the city, but no phone number.
  3. Analysts get what they need, and a leak of the mart reveals no phone numbers.

Answer. The safest personal data is the data that is not copied.

Watch out

Hashing is not anonymisation. A hashed phone number can often be reversed by hashing every possible number. Treat pseudonymised data as personal data unless experts confirm otherwise.

Common mistakes

  • Giving everyone admin access 'to save time'.
  • Copying production personal data into test environments.
  • Credentials in code or in chat messages.
Try it yourself: What is least privilege?

Model answer. Giving each person or service only the access they need for their job, and no more.

Check what you just learned

1. Least privilege means:
  • Everyone is admin
  • Shared passwords
  • No access at all
  • Only the access needed for the job (correct)

Limit access to what is needed.

2. Hashing a phone number:
  • Does not guarantee anonymity (correct)
  • Always makes it anonymous
  • Deletes it
  • Compresses it

Treat it as personal data.
keyPoints: Use least privilege, role-based access, encryption, secrets management, masking and audit logs.
Minimise, separate, mask and tag personal data; plan for deletion.
Privacy laws such as the DPDP Act 2023 and GDPR apply; involve legal and privacy teams.

topics.title: Cost, performance and a design document
topics.html:
Cloud data platforms charge for storage, compute and data movement, so engineering choices are cost choices.

Cost and performance habits
HabitWhy it saves money
Select only the columns you need (not SELECT *)Columnar engines read only those columns
Filter on the partition columnPartition pruning reads far less data
Process incrementallyDo not reprocess years of history every night
Pre-aggregate heavy, repeated queriesCompute once, read cheaply many times
Right-size compute and shut down idle clustersYou pay for what runs
Set lifecycle rules on storageMove or delete old, rarely used data
Monitor spend and set budgets and alertsCatch a runaway query within hours, not at month end

Before building, write a short design document. It forces clear thinking and lets others review it before the work is done.

What a pipeline design document contains

  • Purpose: the business question and who uses the result.
  • Sources: systems, formats, volumes, and any contract.
  • Layers and models: raw, staging, marts; the grain of each fact; the key dimensions (and any slowly changing ones).
  • Processing: batch or streaming, schedule, incremental logic and how it stays idempotent.
  • Quality tests: which checks run, and what happens on failure.
  • Security and privacy: who can see what, personal data handling.
  • Operations: monitoring, alerting, backfills, runbook.
  • Cost and risks: expected cost and what could go wrong.
Worked example

A design in five sentences

A daily revenue mart for the shop.

  1. Purpose: finance needs daily revenue by customer city, ready by 07:00.
  2. Sources: the order-events log (CDC, at-least-once) and customer change history.
  3. Model: dedupe events to the latest status; revenue counts delivered orders; city is the customer's city on the order date (SCD type 2).
  4. Processing: nightly incremental batch, idempotent by order id, backfill by date.
  5. Quality and ops: not-null and unique keys, volume check, alert to the owner by 07:30.

Answer. A short, specific document is far more useful than a long vague one.

Watch out

Cost surprises usually come from one bad query or one forgotten cluster. Set budgets and alerts early, and review the most expensive queries every week.

Common mistakes

  • SELECT * on wide tables in production queries.
  • Never turning off idle compute.
  • Building before writing down the purpose, sources and checks.
Try it yourself: Which two habits most reduce data scanned in a large table?

Model answer. Selecting only the needed columns, and filtering on the partition column.

Check what you just learned

1. A design document should cover:
  • Only the logo
  • Purpose, sources, model, processing, tests, security, operations and cost (correct)
  • Only code
  • Nothing

It makes the design reviewable.

2. Which habit reduces cost?
  • SELECT * everywhere
  • Never stopping clusters
  • Filtering on the partition column (correct)
  • Reprocessing all history nightly

Reading less data costs less.

Key terms: flip and sort

Data quality dimension
Completeness, validity, uniqueness, consistency, timeliness, accuracy.
Lineage
Where data came from and what depends on it.
Least privilege
Only the access needed.
Masking
Hiding identifying values.
Retention
How long data is kept.
Design document
A written plan for a pipeline.
Lifecycle rule
Automatic moving or deleting of old data.
keyPoints: Control cost by reading less (columns, partitions), processing incrementally and pre-aggregating.
Right-size compute, set lifecycle rules, and monitor spend with budgets.
Write a design document covering purpose, sources, model, processing, tests, security, operations and cost.
